\title{Does Query-Adaptive Weighting Help? An Empirical Study of Semantic--Chromatic Fusion\\for Colour-Sensitive Product Image Retrieval}
\author{\todo{authors}}\date{}
\begin{document}\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
Frozen pretrained encoders retrieve semantically correct but often wrongly coloured products, while colour descriptors fail the other way. We study fusing a frozen semantic embedding (CLIP ViT-B/32 or DINOv2-B) with a colour histogram when relevance requires the same article type \emph{and} the same human-annotated colour (Fashion Product Images, small; about 1.8k test queries and 16k gallery images per split; five random splits). A validation-tuned fixed weight raises precision@10 from 0.44 to 0.50 (CLIP) and from 0.34 to 0.49 (DINOv2) at a cost of 2--3 points of category relevance. A training-free query-adaptive weighting rule is practically equivalent to the tuned fixed weight (all mean differences below 0.003 in mAP and P@10; paired confidence intervals within $\pm0.01$ in every split under mAP-based selection). Pixel-based colour similarity predicts human colour labels only moderately (ROC-AUC 0.62--0.74), and a common pixel colour-consistency metric saturates at permissive thresholds. Fusion helps saturated colours most and metallic colours least, and under query-side perturbations the fused ranker inherits the colour histogram's photometric fragility. Relevance is class-level and labels are coarse; we discuss the limits.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Content-based retrieval with frozen pretrained encoders returns semantically correct but often wrongly coloured items; colour descriptors have the opposite failure \cite{TODO}.
Weighted fusion of the two is standard \cite{TODO}; query-adaptive weighting is a frequently proposed refinement \cite{TODO}.
We ask: (RQ1) how much do semantic and chromatic cues complement each other when relevance requires both category and colour; (RQ2) does a training-free query-adaptive weighting add anything beyond a carefully validated fixed weight; (RQ3) do pixel-based colour-consistency metrics agree with human colour labels; (RQ4) where does colour fusion help, and how does it behave under query perturbations; (RQ5) what does it cost.
\textbf{Contributions.} (i) A controlled comparison of fixed and query-adaptive fusion under matched tuning budgets with paired confidence intervals over five splits and two encoders; (ii) evidence on the validity of pixel-based colour metrics against human labels; (iii) breakdowns by colour, robustness and cost; (iv) open code and a disclosed protocol log. We make no claim of a new method.

\section{Problem Formulation}
Let $q$ be a query and $x$ a gallery image. $S_{sem}(q,x)$ is cosine similarity of frozen embeddings; $S_{chr}(q,x)$ is the Bhattacharyya coefficient between square-rooted histograms (HSV $16{\times}4{\times}4$ primary; Lab $4{\times}8{\times}8$ ablation) over a central elliptical region. Both are globally $z$-normalised using validation-pair statistics only.
\textbf{Relevance.} An image is relevant if it has the same article type \emph{and} the same human-annotated base colour as the query (class-level, not instance-level). Semantic relevance@K is the share of the top $K$ with the query's article type; colour match@K the share with the query's colour label. As a secondary measure, pixel colour consistency@K uses CIEDE2000 between median foreground Lab colours below a threshold $\tau$ (percentile of same-class validation pairs). Since relevance is the conjunction of category and colour label, joint label precision@K coincides with $P@K$.

\section{Methods Compared}
\emph{Fixed fusion}: $S=\lambda z_{sem}+(1-\lambda)z_{chr}$, $\lambda$ on a 21-point validation grid.
\emph{Adaptive fusion (reference rule)}: for each query, take its $N$ most semantically similar gallery items; $\alpha(q)\propto\lambda_0\sigma_s^{\gamma}$, $\beta(q)\propto(1-\lambda_0)\sigma_c^{\gamma}$, with $\sigma_s,\sigma_c$ the standard deviations of the normalised scores in that pool. $\gamma=0$ recovers fixed fusion, and the adaptive search grid contains every fixed configuration (search-budget parity). We make no novelty claim for this rule \todo{state after literature check}.
\emph{Selection objectives} (validation only): mAP (primary) and $P@10$ (secondary, added after a first exploratory run).

\section{Experimental Setup}
\textbf{Data.} Fashion Product Images (small) \cite{TODO}; classes with $\ge30$ images per (article type, colour) kept; random image-level validation/test split with five seeds (about 1.8k test queries and 16k gallery images each; the seeds' test sets overlap, so the spread reflects split variation, not independent samples). \textbf{Encoders.} Frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 and DINOv2-B (CLS). \textbf{Metrics.} mAP, R@1, P@10, semantic relevance@10, colour match@10, with 95\% bootstrap CIs over queries and paired differences per run. \textbf{Robustness.} Query-side brightness, contrast, saturation, hue shift, blur, occlusion at four fixed severities; gallery unchanged. \textbf{Cost.} CPU brute-force scoring latency and per-image storage.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Semantic and chromatic cues are complementary (RQ1)}
\input{tables/table_main.tex}
With a validation-tuned weight, fusion improves over the semantic encoder alone on every relevance metric except category relevance (Tables~\ref{tab:main},\ref{tab:fusion}): P@10 rises by +0.057 (CLIP) and +0.156 (DINOv2), human-label colour match@10 by +0.080 and +0.198, and mAP by +0.027 and +0.059, each with paired CIs excluding zero in 5/5 splits; category relevance@10 falls by only 0.019 and 0.027. Colour-only retrieval has P@10 of 0.256 because it ignores category. Relative to colour-only retrieval, fusion adds little in human-label colour match (+0.016 CLIP, 4/5 splits; +0.005 DINOv2, 1/5), i.e.\ fusion keeps the colour descriptor's colour match while adding category. Replacing HSV by Lab histograms changes P@10 by $-0.007$ (CLIP) and $-0.020$ (DINOv2) and lowers human-label colour match; it raises pixel-based Joint@10 (Table~\ref{tab:main}), a reminder that the metric choice matters (\S\ref{sec:metric}).
\input{tables/table_fusion_vs_single.tex}
\begin{figure}[t]\centering\includegraphics[width=.62\linewidth]{figures/fig4_tradeoff.png}\caption{Semantic--colour trade-off under fixed fusion ($\lambda$ swept in steps of 0.1 on the test set; reported, not tuned; one line per seed). Colour match plateaus over a wide $\lambda$ range, then falls sharply as the semantic weight approaches 1.}\end{figure}

\subsection{Query-adaptive weighting adds nothing measurable (RQ2)}
\input{tables/table_paired.tex}
Against the validation-best fixed weight under mAP selection, the adaptive rule differs by at most 0.0026 in absolute mean difference on any metric, and the paired 95\% CI lies within $\pm0.01$ for mAP and $P@10$ in 5/5 splits for both encoders (Table~\ref{tab:paired}). Under $P@10$-based selection the picture is the same except one DINOv2 split, where selection noise yields a $-0.0375$ mAP difference (4/5 splits inside the margin). Validation chose $\gamma{=}0$ (identical to fixed fusion) in 6 of 10 runs under mAP selection and 4 of 10 under $P@10$ selection. Against the untuned $\lambda{=}0.5$, the adaptive rule is simply a different point on the same trade-off curve: +0.015 mAP and +0.028 category relevance but $-0.018$ colour match for CLIP (5/5 splits). The choice of selection objective moves the operating point more than adaptivity does: for CLIP, $\lambda{=}0.5$ and the mAP-selected weight have the same $P@10$ (0.497 vs.\ 0.498) but differ by 0.019 in colour match and 0.016 in mAP.

\subsection{Pixel colour similarity is only a moderate proxy for human colour (RQ3)}\label{sec:metric}
\input{tables/table_metric_agreement.tex}
On random query--gallery pairs, the ROC-AUC for predicting human colour-label agreement is 0.62 (HSV), 0.66 (Lab) and 0.74 (CIEDE2000 of median foreground colour); restricting to same-category pairs raises these to 0.69, 0.71, 0.77. Semantic cosine is near chance (0.54--0.57). This is agreement, not proof that pixels are wrong: labels are coarse and sometimes ambiguous (e.g.\ Grey and Navy Blue have low human-label match even for colour-only retrieval), which caps attainable AUC. The pixel colour-consistency metric also depends heavily on its threshold (Table~\ref{tab:tau}): with $\tau$ at the 90th percentile of same-class validation pairs ($\approx$30.7 $\Delta E_{00}$) it saturates (semantic-only 0.92, colour-only 0.99 for CLIP), whereas at the 25th percentile ($\approx$7.2) it separates the methods (0.35 vs.\ 0.65). We therefore report human-label colour match as primary.
\input{tables/table_tau_sensitivity.tex}

\subsection{Where does fusion help, and how robust is it? (RQ4)}
\input{tables/table_colour_group_gain.tex}
Fusion helps chromatic queries more than achromatic ones in both encoders (colour match gain: CLIP +0.096 vs.\ +0.064; DINOv2 +0.248 vs.\ +0.151), though chromatic queries also leave more headroom. Per colour (CLIP, pooled over splits, descriptive only), gains are largest for Yellow (+0.28), Orange (+0.16), Red (+0.14) and Purple (+0.13) and near zero for Silver, Steel and Gold.
\input{tables/table_robustness_worst.tex}
Under query-side perturbations (Table~\ref{tab:robust}), colour-only retrieval is fragile to photometric changes (retaining 0.20--0.34 of clean P@10) but tolerates blur well (0.71 retained for both encoders' runs; for CLIP it is the most blur-tolerant method, for DINOv2 on par with the fused ranker at 0.72). The fused ranker mostly tracks the semantic encoder for CLIP, but for DINOv2 it retains less of its clean performance than DINOv2 alone under brightness, contrast, saturation and occlusion (e.g.\ 0.70 vs.\ 0.92 under brightness), because it inherits the colour histogram's photometric sensitivity; in absolute worst-case P@10 it still matches or exceeds semantic-only in 11 of 12 encoder--transform pairs, the exception being CLIP under hue shift (0.296 vs.\ 0.304), where the query's colour has intentionally changed. CLIP semantic retrieval is itself fragile to blur and occlusion (0.17 and 0.19 retained). Hue shift changes the intended colour and is not a nuisance; the drop is expected. Robustness values are means over splits without per-condition CIs.

\subsection{Cost (RQ5)}
\input{tables/table_latency.tex}
Adaptive scoring costs about 0.12 ms per query on CPU against 0.03 ms for fixed fusion (brute force over about 16k gallery images; encoder inference excluded), and the colour histogram adds 1 KB per gallery image to a 2--3 KB embedding.

\section{Limitations and Ethical Considerations}
Relevance is class-level (article type $\times$ colour label), not exact-product; images are low resolution; colour labels are coarse and noisy; a single dataset and a single colour descriptor family; frozen encoders only; splits are random at image level and the five seeds overlap, so the reported spread understates uncertainty about new data; seven metrics are compared without multiplicity correction; robustness lacks per-condition CIs. Several analyses were added after a first exploratory run (protocol log in the repository). No external validation yet \todo{another dataset}. Dataset licence and redistribution terms \todo{verify}.

\section{Conclusion}
On colour-sensitive product retrieval with frozen encoders, a validation-tuned fixed semantic--colour weight captures essentially all the benefit we could measure, a training-free query-adaptive weighting does not improve on it, and the choice of tuning objective and colour metric matters more than adaptivity. \todo{Refine after literature check and optional external validation.}
